#6152. The Boeing Jet Already Sitting In American Airlines' Fleet That Could Quietly Replace Its 47 Oldest Widebodies

Michael Derrer Fuchs | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

In June 2026, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom confirmed that his airline has issued formal Requests for Proposals to Boeing and Airbus for a new widebody order. This was unexpected, as American Airlines has increasingly been focused on its domestic network while keeping the long-haul routes to a minimum.

What's more, the order is reported to serve as a replacement for the carrier's Boeing 777-200ER fleet, which was previously believed to be slated for full cabin refurbishments. Meanwhile, the contest hardly appears to be competitive. American Airlines is a major customer for both Boeing and Airbus, but only on the narrowbody side.

With the widebody fleet, the airline has consolidated to just the Boeing 777 and 787, while removing its 767 and Airbus A330 fleet during the pandemic. Multiple factors go into large-scale orders, but the challenge for Airbus is that American already has an ideal 777 replacement in its fleet with the Boeing 787, and it'll be an uphill battle for Airbus to win this order, a challenge that it might not want to tackle.

American Airlines currently has 137 widebodies in its fleet, split between 67 777s and 70 787s. It also has another 19 787-9s on order, which are purely for expansion. As a point of comparison, Delta Air Lines operates 179 widebodies and has 84 firm orders for new widebodies, while United Airlines flies 237 widebodies and has another 134 incoming.

American is strong in Latin America, but the long-haul network is otherwise quite modest, and it's generally accepted that American is suffering for it. At the same time, American operates 47 777-200ERs that were largely delivered between 1999 and 2003, with two more units having arrived in 2006. In other words, there are only two 'young' 777-200ERs in the carrier's fleet, with the rest of them set to reach 30 years of age by the 2030s.

In addition, they also feature oddball Rolls-Royce Trent 800 engines with no commonality to anything else in the carrier's fleet, and they're the airline's least efficient widebody aircraft. Previously, American had planned to refurbish all 47 of these planes with its new Flagship Suites and a more premium layout, but given that it is now looking for replacements, these plans seem uncertain.

What's more likely to occur is that some of the 777-200ERs will be refurbished, and the new widebodies will replace the oldest examples, while also providing some growth. Future deliveries or a possible option order will replace the remaining 777-200ERs in the late 2030s.

Undoubtedly, Boeing's primary offering will be the 787. American has already ordered a total of 89 examples, split between 37 787-8s and 52 787-9s. Notably, American does not operate the 787-10, which is generally positioned as Boeing's replacement for the 777-200ER in terms of size. While American could also look at the 777X, the smaller 777-8 is uneconomical, while the 777-9 is simply massive.

It only has a chance if American is looking to replace its young 777-300ER fleet early or grow its fleet of large flagship widebodies. There is no indication of either. On the Airbus side, the manufacturer sells the A330neo and the A350, with the A330-900 and A350-900 being the primary variants in consideration. The A330-800 is too small to serve as a replacement for the 777, and the A350-1000 is largely the same size as the 777-300ER.

On paper, the A350-900 appears to be the most obvious candidate, as it carries slightly more passengers than the 777-200ER while flying significantly further, a quality that the 787-10 cannot match. Reportedly, however, American is taking a good look at the A330-900. The aircraft is only slightly smaller than the 777-200ER, while possessing excellent range.

The real benefit of the A330-900, however, is that it's generally less expensive to acquire than either the A350 or 787, and availability is better than either model. If American is looking to grow its long-haul network in the near future, the A330-900 is the best aircraft to accomplish that from a timeline perspective, and it can serve as an effective 777 replacement. However, the problem lies with its current fleet.

The 787-10 has sold fewer than 400 examples, and its only US operator is United.

The Boeing 787-9 is virtually the same size as the A330-900 (in other words, just slightly smaller than the 777-200ER). The 787-9 has a longer range and is significantly more fuel-efficient on ultra-long-haul routes, but the two types are extremely competitive on shorter missions. This appears to be a plus for the A330-900, as American primarily uses the 777-200ER for relatively short flights, but the problem for Airbus is that American already flies the 787.

American is a large enough airline that it can support large fleets of multiple types, but the current management team has been focused on fleet simplicity. It currently only operates four aircraft types, and it previously removed the A330 during the pandemic. The A330-900 is a cheaper plane that's available sooner.

However, American would also need to spend money to retrain pilots, retrain maintenance staff, and reestablish a parts pool, all for a plane that's less capable and burns more fuel on the 12-hour flights than the 787-9s that American already flies. The A350-900 is an excellent aircraft that burns only slightly more fuel than the 787 while being far more capable.

However, American barely uses the 777-200ER on ultra-long-haul routes. The primary use of this fleet is trunk routes to Europe and South America, routes where the A350-900 begins to look expensive compared to the 787-9. The 787-9 is cheaper to acquire and is already operating in American's fleet, whereas the A350-900 would be more expensive and would come with significant integration costs.

The 787 is a familiar aircraft type to American, which already operates in large numbers. The A350-900 is larger than the 787-9 and can therefore offer the same or slightly more seats than the 777-200ER, but this assumes that American even wants to maintain its current capacity levels on certain routes.

The size difference between the 787-9 and 777-200ER isn't dramatic, while American could easily make more money by flying the smaller Dreamliner due to its low operating costs. Meanwhile, on the routes where American wants to maintain or increase capacity, Boeing has the 787-10. Apart from the fuselage length, it's identical to the 787-9, and the aircraft has nearly the same operating costs as its smaller sibling.

While it has less range than either the 777 or A350, American seldom pushes the 777 to its limits, and the 787-10 can operate nearly any route that the airline flies the 777-200ER on. On routes like DFW to Tokyo, the 787-9 may suffice. The A330-900 and A350-900 each have strong advantages.

However, the equation becomes difficult when considering how American actually uses its 777-200ER fleet, its current trajectory, and the large established fleet of Dreamliners. Of course, pricing is a major factor in any order, and an attractive offer from Airbus could easily result in American flying A330neos or A350s. However, perhaps the biggest issue with this order is that Airbus likely doesn't want to offer American such an attractive deal.

The A350 is one of the great modern success stories. Orders have been piling up in recent years, as the plane proves itself to be simultaneously cost-effective and capable, able to efficiently operate short transatlantic crossings or the world's longest flights, and Airbus knows this.

Demand is as high as ever, which means that Airbus can charge more money, and the A350 has a growing backlog while Airbus can't build the planes fast enough. The A330neo is a slow seller, but Airbus has been receiving increasingly more orders, and the backlog is growing. Airbus also isn't looking to dramatically boost A330neo production in the future.

Fundamentally, the A330neo exists as a way to capitalize on the high demand for mid-size widebodies with low development costs and keep existing A330 customers. It's a cost-effective solution for its customers given the high degree of commonality with prior A330 models, and Airbus appears content to let A330neo orders trickle in slowly, but steadily.

Meanwhile, Rolls-Royce (the exclusive engine supplier for both programs) has been focused on ensuring that each sale is profitable for the company. This has led some airlines to criticize it for high pricing, but the strategy is proving successful because the planes are in high demand, meaning that the engines are in high demand, and it already has a large backlog that will take years to clear. In short, neither party is in a position where they need to win the American Airlines order.

It's certainly possible that American Airlines will go with Airbus, as fleet diversification allows the carrier to optimize route economics to a greater extent and protects the airline from issues with an aircraft type. In this case, however, neither the A330-900 nor the A350-900 is a clear favorite based on attributes, which means that pricing will be the biggest factor.

While selling the A330-900 or A350-900 also gives Airbus inroads to sell more high-margin widebodies to American in the future, the manufacturer is ultimately more concerned with direct profits rather than market share. Boeing, meanwhile, is incentivized to price more aggressively on this order to keep Airbus from snatching future business with American Airlines.

In addition, the Boeing 787 itself is the front-runner based on attributes, while the 787-10 would prove highly effective. Only time will tell which party American will choose, but in this race, Boeing is the incumbent that is likely aiming to keep Airbus out of the door, while the European manufacturer is the outsider with products that don't fit as cleanly and a smaller appetite to offer low prices.

#6151. Alaska Airlines Launches Global Concierge—Its Answer To United Global Services And American ConciergeKey

Alaska Airlines has started inviting customers into Atmos Global Concierge, its new unpublished invitation-only top tier status along the lines of United Global Services, American Airlines ConciergeKey and Delta 360. The first reports point to an effort to win expensive international business class tickets, with benefits that include a next-flight guarantee during travel disruptions, dedicated assistance and Avis Chairman’s Club. Some of the early reaction has been that the benefits look underwhelming. I disagree. I used to have Avis Chairman’s Club, and it was special. And American’s next-flight guarantee came through for me when I needed it, having this benefit at Alaska could be really clutch. Invitations started surfacing November 9. One recipient shared this language: As one of our most valued status holders, you’ve been selected for two exceptional privileges: a complimentary upgrade to Atmos Titanium status and an inaugural membership in Atmos Global Concierge, our most elevated level of service. The invitation emphasizes travel across Europe, Asia and Oceania, backed by a dedicated team. Global Concierge membership begins immediately and runs through December 31, 2027. You’re invited to ATMOS GLOBAL CONCIERGE by u/iZoooom in AlaskaAirlines Alaska is giving these customers Titanium status and Global Concierge membership. What Atmos Global Concierge Members Get An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion. Direct access to a concierge team. Proactive itinerary monitoring. A next-flight guarantee. Arrival assistance at destinations in Asia, Europe and Oceania. A car transfer at London Heathrow for tight connections. Upgrade priority on global flights. CLEAR+ membership. Avis Chairman’s Club. Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. #6150. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

If you’ve flown ANA’s new 777s, what was your experience like?

#6148. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

#6146. New Bilt Deals With Hyatt, Marriott And Sports Team Reveal Bigger Bet On Rewards Across Your Whole Neighborhood

Bilt wants the building you live in, the hotel program you belong to, and the team you root for to get you recognized and rewarded at businesses around you. Its new Neighborhood OS and membership platform bring together merchants, housing communities, Hyatt, Marriott and professional sports teams in a much bigger play than earning points on rent. The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back. I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use. There are two pieces to the announcement: Tools for merchants. Neighborhood OS connects the reservation, payment, point of sale and loyalty systems a business already uses. The goal is to help it recognize customers, deliver benefits, bring in new business and encourage repeat visits. Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it. The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals! “Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent. Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry. We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched. Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest. Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert). And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants: Find customers who can become regulars. A restaurant with empty tables on Tuesday can reach people in nearby buildings who are deciding where to eat. Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full. Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people. Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount. There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. Bilt’s tech is better than what others have tried in the past. Here’s Bilt’s illustration of the merchant experience: The artificial intelligence component isn’t just buzz marketing. They can handle requests and coordinate actions across systems that otherwise require staff to do the work manually. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly. Bilt’s merchant sales page lists a $495 monthly Neighborhood OS subscription and an optional $195 monthly Neighborhood Marketplace subscription, or $690 for both. It lists a $1,500 onboarding fee waived through December 31, 2026. Bilt says members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local merchants over the last year. A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business. Sports fans. The Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury plan to launch in spring 2027 inside their existing app including concession offers, the ability to purchase seat upgrades when inventory opens, and neighborhood benefits connected to team wins. A fan concierge could help with a ride after the game or a restaurant offer nearby. Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner. Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns. Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use. Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit. I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time. Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive. They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly. This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

They want to be a middleman and they’ve done payment processing for some big landlords. Exciting. Unfortunately, their 2026 was a complete disaster – dumped by a real bank, picked up by PE who wanted pie in the sky but instead got 3 versions of a credit card in 8 months that never achieved any market penetration. On the heels of that failure they’re pulling the rug out from the only part of the credit card that offered a bit more value to consumers than they could get from reliable banks.

All that means is that the marketing dollars they put into their growth plan did not result in more growth, so the marketing dollars had to be cut off because the hockey stick growth that would have supported the charade never materialized.

Now, of course, they have PE investors that would like to make some money off of this failure. So what do they do? They have some digital infrastructure that is underutilized and that they’d like to more broadly deploy. So back to basics… meaningless puffery and branding! They’re trying to refocus on the “meh” stuff that they originally did, because when pie in the sky fails, that’s what you do. Notably absent from this announcement though are any real, meaningful partnerships for “the Neighborhood OS”. Such branding and hubris.

Anyway, good news everyone, our neighborhoods are about to be brought together like never before by Bilt’s amazing AI capabilities… you know, the ones that couldn’t even answer questions about its own program accurately? In fairness, Bilt executives couldn’t answer questions about its own program accurately, so seems harsh to blame the AI.

Enjoy the grandfathering while it lasts, folks.

Wuttt. This was supposed to be a big jetBlue announcement day. So much for that… Oof. So, they’re now pulling an Allbirds, Boom Supersonic “but, but, actually, we’re now an AI company”? Very 2024/2025 of them. I think they missed the gravy train on that one.

If Bilt and Hyatt really want to make a difference, allow their hotel bookings through Bilt to qualify for EQN like Amex FHR program does.

That will make me want to stay at Hyatts using Bilt.

This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

Re Sports teams sponsorships, hopefully they only view it as an advertising for new customers /sponsorship sort of thing. I have no interest in redeeming my points for watching overpriced US franchises.

@Too many – I think Bilt has been talking about that exactly

Remember, all of this is only worth $620, less than most other cards. Frequent Miler says so, and thye are so omniscient they don’t even need facts to prove it.

At the end of the day, loyalty programs operate within the razor-thin margins of retail. Why would these businesses fund rewards for another ecosystem instead of their own?

No amount of corporate spin can hide the obvious: Bilt bought market share with a credit card point system they certainly lost money on. Pretending it’s business genius to attract cardholders when you literally paid for them to be your customer is a choice.

“And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g., a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert).”

I love this fairy tale of “integrated rewards” where one credit seamlessly leads to another in a virtuous cycle. That is completely disconnected from how consumers actually behave. Nobody plans a night out three months in advance around stringing together a free Lyft, a free appetizer, and an ice cream.

People burn rewards when they get them or hoard them for flight. Marketers love drawing neat, circular diagrams of loyalty ecosystems, but real usage is jagged.

And sports? Live entertainment and sports are notorious for offering terrible value. At this point, it’s literally cheaper to take my girlfriend to Italy than it is to buy a decent seat at MSG against a competitor.

Hotel Loyalty? Once everyone is special, no one is.

And Grubhub? It’s the bottom of the barrel among delivery platforms. Every single party in the food delivery economy is miserable: consumers get gouged by markups and fees, drivers make pennies, and restaurants watch their margins get stripped away.

Want a real loyalty program? Become a regular at your local neighborhood spot. Get to know the owner, the bartenders, and the staff. You’ll get far more genuine hospitality, comped drinks, and a sense of community by supporting a local business than you ever will churning points.

@L3 — Bahaha… I love that you cannot let that go… L3 again… never change!

Not sure how they’ll get this to work considering every time I try to use Bilt Checkout at the handful of places listed in the app I get a confused stare

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

When it comes to earning credit card rewards, sometimes two cards really are better than one.

Maybe you have a card that earns bonus points on dining and groceries but falls short on other everyday purchases. Or perhaps you love your card's travel perks but wish it offered better earning rates outside of travel.

That's where pairing cards can come in handy. By choosing two cards with complementary benefits and earning categories, you can get more out of your spending without relying on a single card for everything.

Here are three American Express card combinations worth considering, depending on your spending habits and travel goals.

Frequent travelers who want a combination of premium travel benefits and strong everyday earning rates may get the most value from pairing the with the .

The Platinum is, at its core, a travel and lifestyle card that offers access to an extensive network of airport lounges worldwide through the Global Lounge Collection, along with a range of statement credits and other travel benefits.

The Gold fills an important gap in the Platinum's earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $50,000 and $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, respectively*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

By using the Platinum for eligible flights and the Gold for dining and groceries, you can earn elevated rewards across several major spending categories while enjoying premium travel benefits. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can also combine your rewards into one balance to use toward travel through Amex's transfer partners (after linking your accounts online).

The trade-off of this card combination is cost. The Platinum has an $895 annual fee, while the Gold has a $325 annual fee, bringing the combined annual cost to $1,220. For that reason, I'd only recommend this pairing to travelers who can take advantage of the Platinum's benefits and who regularly spend in the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: How these two cards got me over $4,500 in value in one year

If you spend a lot on dining and groceries but want to earn more than 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases, the and could make a great pair.

The Gold earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year*) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year*). It also earns 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

Then, use the Blue Business Plus for eligible business purchases that would earn only 1 point per dollar on the Gold. It earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*) compared with the Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up a single rewards balance to use toward travel through Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Gold has a $325 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee, so you won't pay extra to add a flat-rate earning card to the mix.

Just keep in mind that the Blue Business Plus is a business card, so you'll need to qualify to apply. This combination could be especially useful for freelancers and small-business owners with eligible business expenses that don't fall into the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: The 4 Amex cards I’d use to earn Membership Rewards points faster

If your business spends a lot on things like advertising, software or gas, the and could make a great pair.

The Business Gold earns 4 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in combined purchases per calendar year*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

What I like about the Business Gold is that you don't have to choose your bonus categories in advance. Amex automatically determines your top two eligible categories each billing cycle, which is helpful if your business expenses change from month to month.

For purchases outside those categories, the Blue Business Plus earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*). That's double the Business Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

For example, you might use the Business Gold for advertising and software expenses, then switch to the Blue Business Plus for other eligible business purchases. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up one balance to use with Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Business Gold has a $375 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee. This combination makes the most sense if you spend enough in the Business Gold's bonus categories to justify the annual fee while using the Blue Business Plus to earn more on other purchases.

Related: 7 reasons why the Amex Blue Business Plus Card should be in everyone’s wallet

Before adding another Amex card to your wallet, take a look at where you're spending the most money and what you want to get out of your rewards. The goal is to find a card that fills a gap in your current lineup, rather than one that offers more of the same.

And remember, earning more points isn't worth it if you're spending more than you normally would or carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: Best credit card strategies for couples

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to choosing the best credit card combination. The key is finding cards that complement each other rather than simply offer more of the same benefits.

Whether you're looking for premium travel perks, stronger everyday earning rates or a way to maximize rewards on business expenses, pairing the right Amex cards can help you earn more Membership Rewards points.

Just make sure the additional rewards and benefits are worth the combined annual fees and that you're choosing cards that make sense for your spending habits.

#6143. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?

#6142. United Airlines Pilot Couldn’t Fly After A Stroke—His Union Urged Removal, And His Military Bias Suit Failed

A United Airlines pilot left for military duty in September 2001, planning to come back two years later. Instead, he was furloughed, suffered a stroke, lost his medical clearance and eventually learned that his own union had recommended removing him from the airline’s seniority list. Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions. United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003. Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force. On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke. United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open. His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019. United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September. In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline. Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012. In January 2019, Bumpus sought to return and obtain medical leave to preserve his employment while resolving his medical certification. United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired. He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority. Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023. He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches: United owed him reemployment after military service. This included his argument that it should accommodate his medical condition through leave or an appropriate alternative position. United treated him worse because of his military service. He pointed to other pilots who received leave or returned with their seniority intact. I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role. But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway. What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military. He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. The judge assumed, for purposes of deciding the case, that Bumpus was right about the 2019 deadline. Even with that assumption, he hadn’t shown military bias. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias. The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to. Topics on this pageAir Line Pilots Association, InternationalUniformed Services Employment and Re-employment Rights Act of 1994United AirlinesAmerican AirlinesChicagoDenver+3 more More From View from the Wing

Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions.

United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003.

Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force.

On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke.

United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open.

His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019.

United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September.

In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline.

Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012.

United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired.

He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority.

Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023.

He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches:

I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role.

But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway.

What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military.

He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias.

The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to.

#6140. Delta SkyMiles Gold Card Review: Solid Perks For Occasional Delta Flyers

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card is the mid-range personal credit card in the American Express and Delta co-brand card portfolio, which includes seven cards, covering a variety of annual fee levels, across both personal and business products.

This post is my in-depth review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Amex Card. The card has a reasonable annual fee and is ideal for someone looking for basic benefits that come in handy when flying Delta. However, if you’re a Medallion elite flyer on Delta, another card might be a better option (more on that below).

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card review, here’s a quick look at the card’s main selling points and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Delta Gold Amex welcome bonus and ongoing fees, since these are some of the most important features to consider when opening a new card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex is currently offering new cardholders the following bonus: You may be eligible for as high as 80,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $2,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $880.

This is a solid welcome bonus, though the card recently offered a higher one that included a statement credit along with bonus miles. Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they’d rather wait for a better offer, or apply with this offer so they can take advantage of the perks ASAP.

The welcome offer on the Delta Gold Amex card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past.

You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal versions of the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more) or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the Delta Gold Amex first. That’s because if you do, you’d potentially still be eligible for the Delta Platinum Amex and Delta Reserve Amex. Meanwhile if you apply for one of those cards first, you’d no longer be eligible for the “lesser” card.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score you need to get approved for the Delta Gold Amex. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been denied, as it’s only one of many factors that determines card eligibility.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees). This is a great opportunity to try the card before you have to “buy” it. The card also has a reasonable annual fee on an ongoing basis, so it’s easy to recoup that fee by taking advantage of the card perks.

You can also add authorized users to the Delta Gold Amex at no extra cost.

If you are going to put spending on the card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees) with the Delta Gold Amex, so you can use the card abroad without paying those high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. Unfortunately the Delta Gold Amex isn’t much to get excited about on that front, but let’s still go over the details.

When it comes to the return on spending, the Delta Gold Card offers:

While it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling. There are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays it’s common to see airlines offer elite status qualification through credit card spending. Delta SkyMiles elite status is based on the concept of Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs), and it’s possible to earn elite status with credit card spending.

The catch is that the Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn any MQDs, so if you want to qualify for status, you’ll have to pick up the Delta Platinum Card or Delta Reserve Card. More on that later.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

As I’ll cover below, having the Delta Gold Amex also gives you access to the TakeOff 15 discount on award tickets, and that can also help you stretch your SkyMiles for travel on Delta.

The real reason you’ll want to keep the Delta Gold Card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which are great for the casual Delta flyer. Truthfully, this is the value proposition of many airline credit cards — it’s largely about the welcome bonus and the perks, so let’s take a closer look at those details for the Delta Gold Amex.

Perhaps one of the biggest incentives to actually spend money on the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is the ability to earn a flight credit. Specifically, if you spend $10,000 on the card in a calendar year, you can receive a $200 Delta eCredit to use toward future travel, which will be deposited right in your SkyMiles account. The credit expires one year after it’s issued.

Getting a $200 Delta eCredit in addition to any miles could be a good incentive to spend $10,000 on the card per year. The credit alone is the equivalent of a 2% return on spending, assuming you consider it to be worth face value.

Just for having the Delta Gold Card you receive up to $100 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $100 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $100, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex, you get a first checked bag free. You can also receive a second checked bag free on eligible domestic Delta flights.

This benefit is limited to the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for your flight with your Delta Amex, though you do need to have your SkyMiles number in the reservation.

With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up. A first checked bag on domestic flights costs $45, and a second costs $55, so even just checking one bag on two roundtrip flights could effectively cancel out the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Gold Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary card member’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation. This benefit is valid for the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation.

If you have the Delta Gold Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible inflight purchases of food and beverages. The statement credit will post within 8-12 weeks of an eligible purchase.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for 1.0 cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the Delta TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta flights booked through delta.com or the Fly Delta app. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card also comes with a rideshare credit. The way it works is that you get up to $10 back as a statement credits each month when you use the card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

You need to enroll in this benefit in order to get the money back, and it doesn’t kick in until after your first card renewal. So while it’s a useful perk if you already pay for rideshares at least once a month, it doesn’t really make or break the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in having as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. Note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card isn’t a card I’d be using for my everyday spending, since there are many more rewarding cards for that. However:

In other words, for someone who flies Delta occasionally, I think this card could make sense, and the benefits can more than offset the annual fee.

Meanwhile if you’re a more frequent Delta flyer, there could be value to having one of the more premium credit cards, which allow you to spend your way to elite status, and earn Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs).

If the Delta Gold Card sounds interesting to you, but you want a business card instead, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card. Learn more about applying for Amex business cards.

The Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (learn more) has a $0 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following benefits:

Beyond that, though, there are limited perks. If you’d get value out of a first checked bag free or priority boarding, then you’re much better off getting one of Delta’s cards with an annual fee. I can’t really see much upside to getting the Delta Blue Card, over the other options in the market.

The Delta Platinum Amex (learn more) has a higher annual fee of $350 (Rates & Fees) and offers more perks than the Delta Gold:

If you want to earn MQDs toward elite status and enjoy more Delta benefits, like an annual companion certificate, the Delta Platinum Amex is the better option between these two cards.

The Delta Reserve Card (learn more) is the most premium option among personal Delta Amex cards, with the highest annual fee: $650 (Rates & Fees)

It also has the most benefits, so it could be worth it if you frequently fly Delta and want the best perks like lounge access:

Those aren’t even all the Delta Reserve card benefits. It also lets you earn MQDs on spending and gets you upgrade priority over other Delta SkyMiles members with your same Medallion tier, product, and fare experience purchased. The annual fee is high, but it’s absolutely worth a look if you want as many Delta perks as possible.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers:

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is a card that can be worth holding onto for the benefits that it offers, like up to $100 in Delta Stays credit, free checked bags, priority boarding, inflight savings, and more.

For the more frequent Delta flyer, consider the Delta Platinum Card, which can offer a larger bonus and additional perks, but also has a higher annual fee. Meanwhile if you’re a true Delta frequent flyer, consider the Delta Reserve Card, which offers some lounge access perks, helps you qualify for status fastest, etc.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Gold Amex Card, follow this link.
